clinicalPearls: Refers to herniation of cerebrospinal fluid into the sella turcica, flattening the pituitary against the sellar floor
The primary form arises from a congenitally incompetent diaphragma sellae and is often an incidental imaging finding
The secondary form follows pituitary damage from surgery, radiotherapy, apoplexy, or regression of a tumour or of Sheehan-related infarction
Most people with a primary empty sella have normal pituitary function and no symptoms
It is commonly seen in overweight middle-aged women, and may coexist with idiopathic intracranial hypertension
When present, symptoms include headache and, less commonly, variable degrees of hypopituitarism or mild hyperprolactinaemia from stalk effect
Visual disturbance is unusual but can occur if the optic chiasm prolapses into the sella
Management is largely reassurance and monitoring, with hormone replacement only if genuine deficiencies are demonstrated
reference.pathophysiology: Empty sella describes an enlarged or remodelled sella turcica filled with cerebrospinal fluid, with the pituitary gland compressed against the floor. In the primary form, a defective or incomplete diaphragma sellae allows pulsatile cerebrospinal fluid pressure to be transmitted into the sella, gradually flattening the gland; raised intracranial pressure may contribute. The secondary form results from loss of pituitary volume after infarction, surgery, irradiation or involution of a previously enlarged gland or tumour. Despite the appearance, a rim of functioning pituitary tissue usually persists, so endocrine function is often preserved, although stalk distortion can occasionally impair hormone secretion or mildly raise prolactin.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic pituitary lesion such as a Rathke cleft cyst
Cystic or partially resolved pituitary adenoma
Arachnoid cyst of the sellar region
additionalInvestigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to confirm the empty or partially empty sella
Prolactin measurement to detect stalk-related elevation
Dynamic pituitary testing if deficiency is suspected
Visual field assessment if chiasmal prolapse is a concern
Assessment for raised intracranial pressure where clinically indicated
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss from chiasmal herniation
New pituitary dysfunction after prior pituitary treatment
reference.prognosis: The primary form is usually benign with a normal life expectancy and preserved pituitary function, requiring only reassurance; prognosis in the secondary form depends on the underlying cause and the extent of any hormone deficiency, which is managed with appropriate replacement.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or over-treating an incidental, asymptomatic empty sella
Assuming pituitary function is normal without confirmatory hormone testing when symptoms are present
Missing cortisol deficiency in a symptomatic patient
Failing to distinguish a partially empty sella from a cystic sellar mass
management: Reassurance and no active treatment for the common asymptomatic primary form with normal pituitary function
Baseline and, where indicated, dynamic anterior pituitary testing, with hormone replacement such as thyroxine, glucocorticoid, sex-steroid or growth hormone for any demonstrated deficiency
Dopamine-agonist therapy only where significant hyperprolactinaemia arises from a stalk effect
Management of coexisting idiopathic intracranial hypertension, including weight reduction and acetazolamide, in the typical overweight middle-aged group
Visual field assessment with neurosurgical referral if chiasmal prolapse threatens vision
For the secondary form, treat the underlying cause such as prior surgery, radiotherapy, apoplexy or Sheehan infarction and replace deficient hormones
Endocrinology follow-up to monitor for evolving hypopituitarism
